<reason>Side B (PRO) won a close, high-quality debate. B's coordination-problem frame — the harm is collective, so only a universal default fixes it — survived the whole exchange and was crystallized memorably ("where does the grade live at twelve?"). B's first rebuttal landed the sharpest blow: CON's "defaults for minors" requires the same age gate CON called catastrophic, forcing A to shift to universal defaults, which B then framed as inconsistent scheme-switching and a bigger political fight. B also flipped A's leverage argument (ban creates platform liability like bars) and answered A's pressure questions directly with plausible background knowledge (reasonable-steps liability, existing online age gates, network effects keeping grades off obscure apps). A's best surviving route — the asymmetry-of-stakes surveillance argument (liability drives universal ID checks; defaults only need weak inference) — was genuinely strong and never fully neutralized, and A's "who can still see them" closing was effective. But A slightly overstated the leakage "wash," misattributed a concession to B in the closing, and never squarely answered B's point that a chronological feed leaves the exiled child exiled and the group's social dynamics intact. B made the debate easier to decide and controlled the decisive clash.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1 contradiction: CON's design mandates "for minors" need exactly the age-verification gate CON called a privacy catastrophe — "if verification is catastrophic, CON's plan is catastrophic; if it is workable, the ban is workable." This forced A into the scheme-shift that B exploited for the rest of the debate, and A's universal-defaults escape never fully dissolved the tension between its two versions of the plan.</best_rebuttal>
